evidence.claim: A glacier-carved road corridor links temple stone, silver mines and skiing towns.
evidence.quote: Alta was founded about 1865 to house miners from the Emma mine, the Flagstaff mine, and other silver mines in Little Cottonwood Canyon.

evidence.claim: A glacier-carved road corridor links temple stone, silver mines and skiing towns.
evidence.quote: the access road for Little Cottonwood Canyon and the ski resorts of Alta and Snowbird.

evidence.claim: SR-210 climbs from Little Cottonwood Canyon’s mouth to Alta through a U-shaped valley carved by an alpine glacier.
evidence.quote: The canyon is a glacial trough (U-shaped canyon), carved by an alpine glacier during the last ice age, 15,000 to 25,000 years ago.

evidence.claim: The Forest Service presents the scenic byway as a drive through a rugged, glacially carved corridor.
evidence.quote: Visitors will be awestruck by the sheer ruggedness and beauty of the glacially carved corridor.

evidence.claim: In the lower canyon, smooth, steep rock faces rise several hundred feet.
evidence.quote: The lower third of the canyon is strewn with quartz monzonite, granite, and granodiorite outcroppings, mostly consisting of smooth steep faces, some up to several hundred feet high.

evidence.claim: Visit Utah lists 15 minutes to Alta for its seven-mile byway description.
evidence.quote: 7 miles | 15 minutes to Alta

evidence.claim: The state legislature defined SR-210 in 1941, linking Wasatch Boulevard with the canyon road to Alta.
evidence.quote: The state legislature defined State Route 210 in 1941 to run from SR-4 (US-40, now I-80) at the mouth of Parley's Canyon south along Wasatch Boulevard to Little Cottonwood Canyon, then east through the canyon to Alta.

evidence.claim: In 1975, the Alta Bypass Road joined the route to provide an alternative when snow slides closed the main road.
evidence.quote: The Alta Bypass Road was added to SR-210 in 1975, providing an alternate route when snow slides close the main roadway.

evidence.claim: A proposed mountain connection to Brighton was included in the highway’s legal definition but never built; the route was formally cut back to Alta in 1994.
evidence.quote: The definition of SR-210 was changed in 1969 to absorb this mountainous route, but in 1994 it was truncated back to Alta, the extension having not been constructed.

evidence.claim: Begin at the canyon mouth, where pioneers quarried stone for the Salt Lake Temple.
evidence.quote: At the mouth of the canyon is the site where Mormon pioneers quarried massive granite blocks used to construct the Salt Lake Temple

evidence.claim: Granite Mountain stands one mile up the canyon.
evidence.quote: Granite Mountain is a mass of solid rock one mile up Little Cottonwood Canyon

evidence.claim: Continue to Snowbird, then farther up to Alta, the road’s terminus.
evidence.quote: Travel further up the Little Cottonwood Scenic byway and you will arrive at Utah’s first ski resort, Alta.

evidence.claim: SR-210 climbs from Little Cottonwood Canyon’s mouth to Alta
evidence.quote: State Route 210 is the primary access road to the canyon, running from the canyon mouth up to Alta.

evidence.claim: A proposed mountain connection to Brighton
evidence.quote: State Route 229 was defined in 1941, connecting SR-210 near Alta to SR-152 (now SR-190) near Brighton along a proposed roadway.

evidence.claim: Alta, the road’s terminus.
evidence.quote: The route turns east entering the mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon and continues east and east-northeast before terminating in Alta.

evidence.claim: The lower canyon’s smooth, steep rock faces include quartz monzonite, granite and granodiorite.
evidence.quote: The lower third of the canyon is strewn with quartz monzonite, granite, and granodiorite outcroppings, mostly consisting of smooth steep faces

evidence.claim: Granite Mountain’s name is less precise than its stone: the mass is primarily quartz monzonite.
evidence.quote: Despite its name, Granite Mountain is primarily composed of quartz monzonite

evidence.claim: This igneous rock resembles granite in appearance and composition, and the same material went into the Salt Lake Temple and the facade of the LDS Conference Center.
evidence.quote: an igneous rock similar to granite in appearance, physical characteristics, and chemical composition. This is the same material used to construct the Salt Lake Temple and the facade of the LDS Conference Center.

evidence.claim: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints also excavated a records vault 600 feet into the canyon’s north side.
evidence.quote: a large archive and vault owned by the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS Church) excavated 600 feet into the north side of Little Cottonwood Canyon.

evidence.claim: Its controlled environment holds genealogical records; the church makes records available through Family History Centers and its FamilySearch website.
evidence.quote: a dry, environment-controlled facility used for long-term record storage

evidence.claim: Here, the mountain is both building material and a place for storing records.
evidence.quote: Records stored include genealogical and family history information

evidence.claim: the church makes records available through Family History Centers and its FamilySearch website.
evidence.quote: The church makes the records publicly available through its Family History Centers, as well as online at its FamilySearch website.

evidence.claim: The name Big Emma survives on a ski run in Snowbird’s Gad Valley, carrying a mining name into a different use of the canyon.
evidence.quote: Known as the Emma Mine (the origin of the name of the Big Emma ski run in Snowbird's Gad Valley)

evidence.claim: Silver mining became a major local industry in the nineteenth century.
evidence.quote: Mining became a large local industry, and Little Cottonwood Canyon became one of the largest producers of silver ore in the Wasatch Mountains.

evidence.claim: Ted Johnson, a former manager of Alta Lodge, later explored the Peruvian Gulch and Emma Mine/Gad Valley watersheds below Alta as the setting for Snowbird.
evidence.quote: He had explored the terrain below Alta in the Peruvian Gulch and Emma Mine/Gad Valley watersheds that later became Snowbird.

evidence.claim: He partnered with Dick Bass in 1969, and the ski area opened in December 1971.
evidence.quote: Johnson met Dick Bass, a Texas oilman, in 1969, and the two partnered to create the Snowbird resort, which opened in 1971.

evidence.claim: The community now takes its identity from skiing and summer recreation on land once associated with mining.
evidence.quote: Snowbird is an unincorporated community in Little Cottonwood Canyon

evidence.claim: the ski area opened in December 1971.
evidence.quote: an alpine skiing and snowboarding area, which opened in December 1971.

evidence.claim: The community now takes its identity from skiing and summer recreation on land once associated with mining.
evidence.quote: It is most famous for Snowbird Ski and Summer Resort

evidence.claim: Alta’s change from silver camp to ski town followed a fire, an avalanche and a long decline in mining.
evidence.quote: An 1878 fire and an 1885 avalanche destroyed most of the original mining town, though some mining activity persisted into the 20th century.

evidence.claim: The fire struck in 1878 and the avalanche in 1885, destroying most of the original town.
evidence.quote: An 1878 fire and an 1885 avalanche destroyed most of the original mining town

evidence.claim: By the 1930s, George Watson was its only remaining resident.
evidence.quote: By the 1930s, only one resident, George Watson, remained in the town.

evidence.claim: Facing back taxes on his mining claims, he donated much of his Alta land to the Forest Service with the condition that it become a ski area.
evidence.quote: Facing back taxes on mining claims that he owned, Watson donated much of his land in Alta to the U.S. Forest Service, stipulating that the land be used to construct a ski area.

evidence.claim: Alf Engen was hired in 1935 to help develop it; Alta is now a town centered on the ski area.
evidence.quote: In 1935, Norwegian skiing legend Alf Engen was hired to help develop the area

evidence.claim: Alta is now a town centered on the ski area.
evidence.quote: Today, Alta is a small town centered around the Alta Ski Area.

evidence.claim: Little Cottonwood Creek runs the canyon’s length from Cecret Lake at Alta westward.
evidence.quote: Little Cottonwood Creek runs down the length of the canyon, beginning at Cecret Lake at Alta and flowing westward.

evidence.claim: The watershed supplies drinking water to much of Salt Lake County.
evidence.quote: The Little Cottonwood Canyon watershed provides drinking water to much of Salt Lake County.

evidence.claim: Alta stands at 8,950 feet, among Utah’s highest cities.
evidence.quote: At 8,950 feet (2,730 m), Alta is one of the highest cities in Utah and one of the highest in America.

evidence.claim: In Albion Basin, the canyon also contains rare and endemic plant species.
evidence.quote: A number of rare and endemic plant species are found in the canyon's Albion Basin.

evidence.claim: Ted Johnson, a former manager of Alta Lodge,
evidence.quote: Ted Johnson, who had managed the Alta Lodge in the town of Alta

flags: Visit Utah describes seven miles and 15 minutes; cache 11 describes approximately 8.3 canyon-road miles and cache 02 a 13.62-mile state highway. Retained the tourism body’s attributed estimate without equating these extents.
Cache 17 dates the first Alta lift to 1939; cache 18 says 1938. Omitted the date.
Current minutes-from-downtown wording is supported only by vague tourism copy and is omitted as an unreliable travel estimate.
Snowbird is retained as the existing community moment, focused on mining and changed land use, not a business recommendation.

No vault visitation is established. Cached Forest Service watershed prohibitions on pets and swimming remain valid evidence, but were omitted from this road-history story; no live access check was possible.

Alta’s 8,950-foot elevation and relative height are supported in cache 18 and retained. No current historical claim proved wholly unsupported; omissions concern precision, relevance and conflicting lift dates.
